examples.solution_text:
The denominator is $f(x)=3x^{2}+5x-8$, with derivative $f'(x)=6x+5$. The numerator matches exactly.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{6x+5}{3x^{2}+5x-8}\,dx\\&=\ln|3x^{2}+5x-8|+C\end{aligned}$
This primitive applies on any interval where $3x^{2}+5x-8\ne0$.

For $f(x)=16-x^{2}$, we need $f'(x)=-2x$. Since $3x=-\dfrac{3}{2}(-2x)$, take the constant adjustment outside the integral.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{3x}{16-x^{2}}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\int\dfrac{-2x}{16-x^{2}}\,dx\\&=-\dfrac{3}{2}\ln|16-x^{2}|+C\end{aligned}$

For $f(x)=e^{4x}+7$, we need $f'(x)=4e^{4x}$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{e^{4x}}{e^{4x}+7}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\int\dfrac{4e^{4x}}{e^{4x}+7}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln(e^{4x}+7)+C\end{aligned}$
The denominator is positive for every real $x$, so modulus signs are unnecessary.

examples.question_text:
Find:
a. $\int\dfrac{\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx$
b. $\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{4+\tan x}\,dx$.
examples.solution_text:
a. For $f(x)=6+3\sin x$, we need $f'(x)=3\cos x$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{3\cos x}{6+3\sin x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{1}{3}\ln(6+3\sin x)+C\end{aligned}$
Here $6+3\sin x\ge3$, so the denominator is positive.

b. For $f(x)=4+\tan x$, its derivative $f'(x)=\sec^{2}x$ matches the numerator.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}x}{4+\tan x}\,dx\\&=\ln|4+\tan x|+C\end{aligned}$
This applies on intervals where $\tan x$ is defined and $4+\tan x\ne0$.

examples.question_text: Use $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to evaluate $\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\tan x\,dx$ exactly.
examples.solution_text:
The denominator is $f(x)=\cos x$, with derivative $f'(x)=-\sin x$. The numerator needs a factor of $-1$. Also, $\cos x>0$ throughout $[0,\pi/3]$.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\tan x\,dx\\&=\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx\\&=-\int_{0}^{\pi/3}\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx\\&=\left[-\ln|\cos x|\right]_{0}^{\pi/3}\\&=-\ln\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln1\\&=\ln2\end{aligned}$

For $f(x)=x^{2}+8$, we need $f'(x)=2x$. The denominator is positive throughout the interval.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{3x}{x^{2}+8}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\int_{1}^{2}\dfrac{2x}{x^{2}+8}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\left[\ln(x^{2}+8)\right]_{1}^{2}\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}(\ln12-\ln9)\\&=\dfrac{3}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{3}\\&=\ln\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^{3/2}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\ln(3x))\\&=\dfrac{1}{\ln(3x)}\times\dfrac{3}{3x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{x\ln(3x)}\end{aligned}$
The integrand is exactly this derivative. Since $x>\dfrac{1}{3}$, we have $\ln(3x)>0$.
$\int\dfrac{1}{x\ln(3x)}\,dx=\ln(\ln(3x))+C$

examples.question_text: A curve has gradient $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{8x}{4x^{2}+3}$ and passes through $(0,2)$. Find its equation.
examples.solution_text:
The derivative of $4x^{2}+3$ is $8x$, matching the numerator.
$y=\ln(4x^{2}+3)+C$
Using $(0,2)$:
$\begin{aligned}\ln3+C&=2\\C&=2-\ln3\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}y&=\ln(4x^{2}+3)+2-\ln3\\y&=\ln\dfrac{4x^{2}+3}{3}+2\end{aligned}$

The denominator is zero at $x=2$, which lies inside $[0,3]$. The integrand has a vertical asymptote there.
Although $2x$ is the derivative of $x^{2}-4$, the logarithmic primitive applies only on intervals where the denominator is nonzero. Substituting the endpoints into $\ln|x^{2}-4|$ across this asymptote is invalid. The definite integral is not defined.

examples.derivation: Differentiating 3x²+5x−8 gives 6x+5, so the primitive is ln|3x²+5x−8|+C on intervals excluding its zeros.
The denominator derivative is −2x and 3x=(−3/2)(−2x). Thus the primitive is −(3/2)ln|16−x²|+C; differentiation recovers the integrand.
Differentiating e^(4x)+7 gives 4e^(4x). The required adjustment is 1/4, giving (1/4)ln(e^(4x)+7)+C. The logarithm argument is always positive.

For part a, the denominator derivative is 3cos x, giving (1/3)ln(6+3sin x)+C; its argument is at least 3. For part b, differentiating 4+tan x gives sec²x, giving ln|4+tan x|+C wherever the integrand is defined.
Writing tan x=sin x/cos x gives primitive −ln|cos x|. Cosine stays positive on [0,π/3], so evaluation gives −ln(1/2)+ln 1=ln 2.
The primitive is (3/2)ln(x²+8). Evaluation from 1 to 2 gives (3/2)(ln 12−ln 9)=(3/2)ln(4/3)=ln((4/3)^(3/2)).
The chain rule gives d/dx ln(ln(3x))=(1/ln(3x))(3/(3x))=1/(x ln(3x)). For x>1/3, both logarithms are defined, so the requested primitive is ln(ln(3x))+C.
Integration gives y=ln(4x²+3)+C. The point (0,2) gives C=2−ln 3, hence y=ln((4x²+3)/3)+2. This satisfies both the gradient and the point.
The denominator vanishes at x=2 inside [0,3]. Near 2, the integrand behaves as 1/(x−2), whose one-sided integrals diverge. The ordinary definite integral is therefore undefined.
